prompt: Ten trials each have the same known marginal success chance, but the trials may be dependent. Can their expected total successes still be found by adding those chances?

options.text: Yes, so the full count must also be binomial.
options.explanation: The binomial distribution additionally requires independent trials.

options.text: No: the expected total must be a possible whole-number outcome.
Yes: express the count as indicators and use linearity.
options.explanation: Each indicator’s expectation is its event probability; dependence does not prevent adding means.
Only some operations, such as splitting product expectations, need extra conditions.

workedExample: Create a one-or-zero indicator for each success. Their sum is the count. Adding their expectations gives its mean even though the distribution and variability may differ from an independent-trial model.

prompt: A uniformly shuffled cloakroom return has one correct coat match on average, whatever the positive number of owners. Why does dependence between owners not invalidate this result?

options.text: The average is really the probability of no matches.
options.explanation: An expected count and a zero-count probability are different quantities.

options.text: Expected indicators add even when matches are dependent.
options.explanation: The sum of individual match probabilities determines the mean count.

options.text: The claim means exactly one person matches in every shuffle.
options.explanation: Individual shuffles can have no matches or several.

options.text: Uniform shuffling makes all match indicators independent.
options.explanation: Knowing other matches can constrain the remaining match.

workedExample: Use one indicator for each owner receiving their own coat. Each owner has one favourable coat among all coats. The many small probabilities add to one, while dependence still affects which match totals occur together.
